questions.stem: Which set of criteria is used to define a mineral?
options: Made in a laboratory or in nature, solid, glassy, with any chemical composition at all
Naturally occurring, solid, made of several minerals cemented together by fine clay
Naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, crystalline, with a definite chemical composition
Naturally occurring, organic or inorganic, liquid or solid, made of two or more rock types
questions.explanation: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with an ordered internal (crystalline) structure and a definite chemical composition. A material made of several minerals cemented together is a rock, not a mineral.

questions.stem: Opal from Coober Pedy is made of silica and water but has no ordered arrangement of atoms. How is it classified?
options: As a mineraloid, because it is not crystalline
As a mineral, because it contains silica like quartz
As a rock, because it is mined from sedimentary layers
As an organic material, because it contains water
questions.explanation: Opal is amorphous: its atoms are not arranged in a regular crystal lattice, so it fails the crystalline criterion and is called a mineraloid. Having the same elements as quartz does not make it a mineral, because structure matters too.

questions.stem: Which example shows a limitation of the criteria used to decide whether a substance is a mineral?
options: Quartz in a granite is a natural, crystalline solid with a definite composition
Halite in a salt lake forms naturally from evaporating water as cubic crystals
Feldspar in a basalt forms naturally as crystals when the lava cools and hardens
Calcite in a mollusc shell matches calcite in limestone but is made by an organism
questions.explanation: Shell calcite has the same composition and structure as mineral calcite, but because it is made entirely by a living thing it is usually excluded. Such borderline cases show the criteria do not always sort substances neatly. Quartz, halite and feldspar meet every criterion.

questions.stem: Olivine's composition is written (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, meaning magnesium and iron can substitute for each other in any proportion. How does this fit the definition of a mineral?
options: The composition includes iron, so olivine is an ore rather than a true mineral
The composition is definite within a range, so olivine is still a single mineral
The composition is not fixed, so olivine is a rock made of two separate minerals
The composition changes, so olivine is a mineraloid like opal or volcanic glass
questions.explanation: 'Definite' composition allows elements of similar size and charge to substitute within a fixed crystal structure, so olivine varies between a magnesium end and an iron end. It is one mineral with a variable formula, not a mixture of two minerals.

questions.stem: Synthetic diamonds made in a factory have the same composition and crystal structure as natural diamonds. Why are they not classed as minerals?
options: They are not hard enough to be minerals
They are not crystalline solids at all
They are not naturally occurring
They are not made of a single element
questions.explanation: Minerals must form by natural processes. Synthetic diamonds are crystalline carbon with the same hardness as natural diamond, but their origin in a factory excludes them.

questions.stem: Minerals are grouped mainly according to which feature of their chemical composition?
options: The main negative ion or ion group, such as silicate or carbonate
The colour of the mineral, such as the green minerals or white minerals
The hardness of the mineral, such as the soft or the hard minerals
The rock type they occur in, such as igneous or sedimentary minerals
questions.explanation: Mineral classes are based on the dominant anion or anion group: silicates (SiO4), carbonates (CO3), oxides, sulfides, sulfates, halides, and native elements. Colour and hardness are properties used to identify minerals, not to classify them chemically.

questions.stem: Calcite has the formula CaCO3. To which mineral group does it belong?
options: Sulfides
Phosphates
Carbonates
Silicates
questions.explanation: The CO3 group makes calcite a carbonate. Carbonates react with dilute hydrochloric acid to release carbon dioxide, which is why calcite fizzes in the acid test.

questions.stem: Which pairing of mineral and group is correct?
options: Quartz (SiO2): native element
Haematite (Fe2O3): carbonate
Galena (PbS): sulfide
Halite (NaCl): oxide
questions.explanation: Galena is lead combined with sulfur, so it is a sulfide. Halite is a halide (a chloride), haematite is an oxide, and quartz is a compound of silicon and oxygen, not a native element.

questions.stem: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon, yet diamond is the hardest natural mineral and graphite is one of the softest. Why?
options: Diamond contains impurities that make its carbon atoms harder
Graphite has absorbed water, which softens its carbon atoms
Diamond forms at the surface and graphite forms deep down
Their carbon atoms are bonded in different crystal structures
questions.explanation: In diamond each carbon atom is strongly bonded to four others in a three-dimensional framework. In graphite the atoms form sheets held together only weakly, so the sheets slide. Different structures of the same composition are called polymorphs.

questions.stem: What is the streak of a mineral?
options: The way the mineral breaks along flat planes when it is struck
The way the mineral's surface reflects light, such as glassy or dull
The colour of its powder, seen by rubbing it on unglazed porcelain
The colour of the mineral's surface, seen in bright natural light
questions.explanation: Streak is the colour of a mineral's fine powder. It is more reliable than surface colour, which impurities and weathering can change. The way light reflects off the surface is lustre.

questions.stem: A grey, metallic mineral leaves a red-brown streak and is barely attracted to a magnet. Another dark metallic mineral leaves a black streak and is strongly magnetic. What are they?
options: Haematite and magnetite
Magnetite and haematite
Galena and graphite
Pyrite and galena
questions.explanation: Haematite can look grey or black but always gives a red-brown streak. Magnetite gives a black streak and is the common mineral most strongly attracted to a magnet.

questions.stem: On the Mohs scale, which mineral has a hardness of 7?
options: Talc
Diamond
Quartz
Calcite
questions.explanation: The Mohs scale runs from talc (1) through gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite and orthoclase feldspar to quartz (7), topaz, corundum and diamond (10). Calcite is 3.

questions.stem: A mineral can be scratched by a steel nail but not by a fingernail, and it scratches calcite. Using hardness only, which mineral could it be?
options: Topaz (8)
Fluorite (4)
Gypsum (2)
Quartz (7)
questions.explanation: A fingernail is about 2.5 and a steel nail about 5.5. The mineral is harder than calcite (3) and the fingernail but softer than steel, so fluorite (4) fits. Gypsum can be scratched by a fingernail, and quartz and topaz are harder than steel.

questions.stem: Corundum is 9 and diamond 10 on the Mohs scale, yet diamond is several times harder than corundum when measured with instruments. What does this show about the Mohs scale?
options: It ranks minerals in order but the steps between them are not equal
It is inaccurate, because diamond should really be ranked as number 40
It measures density rather than hardness, so the numbers do not match
It applies only to soft minerals, so it fails for very hard minerals
questions.explanation: The Mohs scale is ordinal: each mineral scratches those below it, but the numbers are ranks, not measurements. The gap between 9 and 10 is far larger than between 1 and 2. The ranking is still correct, so the scale is useful, just not linear.

questions.stem: A clear, colourless mineral breaks into thin, flexible, see-through sheets along one direction. Which mineral is it?
options: Muscovite
Kaolinite
Calcite
Halite
questions.explanation: Muscovite (white mica) has one perfect cleavage, so it peels into thin, flexible sheets. Biotite is the dark mica with the same cleavage. Kaolinite is an earthy clay, and calcite and halite cleave in three directions into blocks.

questions.stem: A student finds a clear crystal that breaks into rhombus-shaped blocks, can be scratched by a steel nail but not by a fingernail, and fizzes in dilute hydrochloric acid. Which mineral is it?
options: Gypsum
Calcite
Quartz
Fluorite
questions.explanation: Three cleavages not at right angles give calcite its rhombohedral shape, and its hardness of 3 lies between a fingernail and steel. Fizzing in acid shows it is a carbonate. Fluorite is harder (4) and does not fizz.

questions.stem: A glassy, grey mineral in granite scratches glass, shows no flat cleavage surfaces and breaks with curved, shell-like surfaces. Which mineral is it?
options: Augite
Quartz
Feldspar
Biotite
questions.explanation: Quartz (hardness 7) scratches glass and has conchoidal fracture rather than cleavage. Feldspar is nearly as hard but shows two good cleavages, which give flat, light-catching faces. Biotite and augite are dark.

questions.stem: Pink feldspar crystals in a granite have flat faces that flash in the light. In a weathered sample of the same granite, the feldspar has become a soft, white, earthy material, but the quartz is unchanged. What is the white material and why did it form?
options: Powdered quartz, formed as the quartz grains broke into fine dust over time
Kaolinite clay, formed as feldspar reacted with water during chemical weathering
Calcite, formed as feldspar dissolved and left carbonate behind in the rock
Muscovite mica, formed as feldspar was heated and squeezed during weathering
questions.explanation: Feldspar reacts with slightly acidic water to form clay minerals such as kaolinite, which are soft and earthy. Quartz resists chemical weathering, so it survives, which is why sand is mostly quartz. Heat and pressure belong to metamorphism, not weathering.

questions.stem: Which property is least reliable for identifying a mineral?
options: Streak
Hardness
Cleavage
Colour
questions.explanation: Small amounts of impurities can give one mineral many colours; quartz, for example, can be clear, white, pink, purple or smoky. Streak, hardness and cleavage depend on composition and structure, so they are more consistent.

questions.stem: Two dark minerals look alike in a rock collection. Mineral X has two cleavages meeting at close to 90 degrees; mineral Y has one perfect cleavage and peels into sheets. What are they?
options: X is biotite, a dark mica, and Y is augite, a pyroxene
X is quartz, a silicate, and Y is calcite, a carbonate
X is magnetite, an oxide, and Y is galena, a sulfide
X is augite, a pyroxene, and Y is biotite, a dark mica
questions.explanation: Augite, a pyroxene, has two cleavages at nearly right angles, giving blocky crystals. Biotite peels into thin sheets along its single cleavage. Quartz has no cleavage, and magnetite and galena are metallic.

questions.stem: A mineral sample has a mass of 26.5 g. When lowered into a measuring cylinder, the water level rises by 10.0 mL. What is its density, and which mineral is most likely?
options: 0.377 g/cm3, quartz
2.65 g/cm3, galena
265 g/cm3, galena
2.65 g/cm3, quartz
questions.explanation: Density = mass / volume = 26.5 g / 10.0 cm3 = 2.65 g/cm3, the density of quartz. Dividing volume by mass gives 0.377, and galena is far denser, at about 7.5 g/cm3.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are in a mass recorded as 0.0450 g?
options: Five
Three
Two
Four
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point, so they are not significant. The 4, the 5 and the final zero are significant; a trailing zero after the decimal point shows the balance measured to that place.

questions.stem: A student measures a mineral's mass as 42.3 g and its volume as 15 mL, then writes its density as 2.82 g/cm3. Which correction is needed?
options: Round it to 3 g/cm3, as answers should have one significant figure
Keep it as 2.82 g/cm3, as the calculator gave more decimal places
Round it to 2.8 g/cm3, as the volume has only two significant figures
Write it as 2.820 g/cm3, as the mass has three significant figures
questions.explanation: In multiplying or dividing, the answer keeps the number of significant figures of the least precise measurement. The volume has two, so the density is 2.8 g/cm3. Adding a zero claims a precision the data do not have.

questions.stem: A measuring cylinder is marked in 1 mL divisions. Which recording of a water level is most appropriate?
options: 30 mL
questions.explanation: A reading is usually estimated to half the smallest division, so 34.5 mL is appropriate. Adding more decimal places claims a precision the cylinder cannot give, and rounding to 30 mL throws away real information.

questions.stem: Why are diamonds used on the tips of drill bits for drilling through hard rock?
options: Diamond conducts electricity very well
Diamond is the densest natural mineral
Diamond dissolves rock as it is heated
Diamond is the hardest natural mineral
questions.explanation: Diamond's hardness of 10 lets it cut and grind every other material, so industrial diamonds make drilling and cutting faster and more efficient. Diamond is not especially dense and is a poor electrical conductor.

questions.stem: Graphite is used in pencils, as a dry lubricant and in electrodes for batteries. Which pair of properties explains these uses?
options: It is transparent in thin sheets, and it is a good electrical insulator
It is very dense and magnetic, and it dissolves quickly in water
Its sheets slide easily over each other, and it conducts electricity
It is extremely hard and resists heat, and it reacts readily with acid
questions.explanation: Weakly bonded sheets of carbon slide off onto paper and reduce friction between surfaces, and electrons move freely within the sheets, so graphite conducts. It is soft, not hard, and is not an insulator.

questions.stem: Thin sheets of muscovite have been used to insulate electrical parts and as heat-resistant windows in stoves. Which properties make it suitable?
options: It splits into thin sheets and resists heat and electric current
It is very hard and dense and can be cut into solid blocks easily
It dissolves in water and leaves a heat-proof film on any surface
It is magnetic and metallic, so it carries current safely to earth
questions.explanation: Muscovite's perfect cleavage gives thin, flexible, transparent sheets, and it does not conduct electricity and withstands high temperatures. It is soft rather than hard and is not metallic.

questions.stem: Kaolinite is mined for making porcelain and as a filler in glossy paper. Which properties make it useful?
options: It is fine-grained and white, and it can be shaped when wet
It is very hard and metallic, so it polishes to a mirror shine
It is magnetic and dense, so it can be separated easily
It fizzes in acid and releases gas that hardens the clay
questions.explanation: Kaolinite is a soft, white clay made of tiny platy crystals, so it is plastic when wet, fires to white porcelain and gives paper a smooth, bright surface. It is neither hard nor metallic, and it does not fizz in acid.

questions.stem: A company needs a mineral for a gentle household scouring cleanser that removes grime from glass and steel without scratching them. Glass and steel have a hardness of about 5.5. Which choice is best?
options: Corundum (9), as it is one of the hardest minerals and lasts for a long time
Talc (1), as it is the softest mineral and would be hard enough to scour metal
Calcite (3), as it is softer than glass and steel but harder than most grime
Quartz (7), as it is harder than glass and steel and scours the surface quickly
questions.explanation: A scouring mineral must be harder than the grime but softer than the surface, or it will scratch it. Calcite fits this. Quartz and corundum are harder than glass and would scratch it, and talc is too soft to scour much at all.

questions.stem: How does carbon-14 form?
options: Cosmic rays produce neutrons that convert nitrogen-14 in the upper atmosphere
Volcanoes release it from deep in the mantle along with ordinary carbon dioxide
Plants make it from carbon-12 during photosynthesis in their green leaves
Bacteria in the soil produce it as they break down dead organic matter
questions.explanation: Neutrons produced by cosmic rays strike nitrogen-14 atoms high in the atmosphere, turning them into carbon-14. This forms carbon dioxide, which spreads through the atmosphere and enters food chains through photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Why does the amount of carbon-14 in an animal's bone begin to fall only after the animal dies?
options: While alive it breathes in carbon-14 that its body stores only in the lungs
While alive it takes in carbon from food, matching the atmosphere's carbon-14
While alive its body makes carbon-14 from nitrogen, replacing what decays
While alive its bones are protected from decay by the surrounding muscle
questions.explanation: A living organism constantly exchanges carbon with its surroundings, through photosynthesis or eating, so its carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio stays the same as the atmosphere's. At death the intake stops, and the carbon-14 already present decays without being replaced.

questions.stem: Charcoal from a hearth layer in a shell midden contains 12.5% of the carbon-14 it had when the wood was living. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. About how old is the charcoal?
options: About 22 900 years
About 5700 years
About 17 200 years
About 11 500 years
questions.explanation: 12.5% is one-eighth, which is three half-lives (100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5%). 3 x 5730 = 17 190, about 17 200 years. Two half-lives would leave 25%, and four would leave 6.25%.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-14 dating limited to material younger than about 50 000 years?
options: After about nine half-lives too little carbon-14 is left to measure reliably
After about nine half-lives all the carbon in the sample has turned to rock
After 50 000 years the carbon-14 starts to increase again from cosmic rays
After 50 000 years bones and shells no longer contain any carbon at all
questions.explanation: 50 000 years is close to nine half-lives, so less than 1% of the original carbon-14 remains, and tiny amounts of contamination swamp the signal. The sample still contains carbon, mostly stable carbon-12.

questions.stem: A 45 000-year-old megafauna bone and a 3000-year-old shell are each contaminated with the same small amount of modern carbon, such as from groundwater. Which statement is correct?
options: The shell's date is affected far more, because it has more carbon-14 to lose
Both dates are affected equally, because the contamination is the same amount
Neither date is affected, because modern carbon contains no carbon-14 at all
The bone's date is affected far more, because it has so little carbon-14 left
questions.explanation: Modern carbon is rich in carbon-14. In a very old sample, which has almost none left, even a little modern carbon greatly raises the carbon-14 level, making the bone appear many thousands of years too young. The shell has plenty of its own carbon-14, so the same contamination changes it far less.

questions.stem: Marine shells from a midden give radiocarbon ages several hundred years older than charcoal from the same layer. What best explains this?
options: Shells decay faster than charcoal, so their carbon-14 is used up more quickly
Ocean water holds old carbon, so shells start with less carbon-14 than the air
Shells absorb carbon-14 from seawater after death, so they look much older
Charcoal loses carbon-12 in the fire, so it gives an age that is too young
questions.explanation: Deep ocean water has been out of contact with the atmosphere for centuries, so the carbon dissolved in seawater has less carbon-14. Shells built from it start out with an apparent age, the marine reservoir effect, of about 400 years on average, varying by region. Charcoal from land plants avoids this.

questions.stem: Why must raw carbon-14 ages be calibrated, for example against tree rings of known age?
options: The amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied over time
The half-life of carbon-14 changes slowly as the Earth gets older
Tree rings contain no carbon, so they give the true age directly
Carbon-14 decays faster in cold climates than it does in warm ones
questions.explanation: The method assumes the atmosphere's carbon-14 level was constant, but it has changed with cosmic-ray intensity and the carbon cycle. Counting tree rings and other annual layers gives true ages to compare with. Half-lives do not change with time or climate.

questions.stem: Which of these could be dated directly by carbon-14?
options: A piece of charcoal
A piece of basalt
An iron spearhead
A quartz crystal
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 dating works only on material that was once living and took in carbon from the atmosphere, such as charcoal, wood, bone, shell or hair. Basalt, iron and quartz were never alive.
